title: Listen (Rule, Prologue)
hook: the Rule begins with listen, with the ear of your heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, many schools: Thomas beside Augustine, Bonaventure and Scotus, and the Church keeping them side by side. Your line was many teachers. What did you find worth keeping from someone outside your usual school? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

Nod. Say mm-hm. Plan your reply while the other person is still talking. Half-listening takes almost no effort, and it can pass for the real thing for a long time. Now a new block begins: the great religious orders of the Catholic Church, the communities of monks, friars and sisters who live under a shared way of life. We start with the Benedictines, and with a small book written for monks in Italy long ago. Its very first word is an instruction. Not pray. Not work. Not obey. Listen. Today's word: Rule.
screen: `HALF-LISTENING.` → `A NEW BLOCK: THE GREAT ORDERS.` → `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Tradition gives the Rule to Saint Benedict, who gathered monks in Italy and wrote a short book to guide their life together. Monks call it simply the Rule. It covers prayer and work, meals and sleep, guests and the sick, and how to settle a quarrel. But it opens like a letter from a father to a son. In Latin: inclina aurem cordis tui. Listen, my son, to the teaching of the master, and bend down the ear of your heart. Bend down the ear. It's the posture of someone leaning in to catch a quiet voice, a parent bent over a cot. And it's the ear of the heart, not just the ears on your head. Benedict means more than hearing sounds. He means letting what you hear reach the place where you decide things. The Prologue goes on to say that this listening should turn into doing, and that the one speaking is finally God. It borrows a line from the Psalms, here in the Douay-Rheims: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts." Notice the order the Rule sets. Before the long list of chapters, before the schedule, before a single bell rings, there's a posture. Lean in. A rule, for Benedict, isn't a cage of instructions. It's a shared way of listening, kept day after day, so that a whole community can hear together. Benedictine monks and nuns still read the Rule aloud together. Each time they come back around to its start, the first thing they hear is: listen.
screen: `A SHORT BOOK FOR MONKS.` · `BEND DOWN THE EAR OF YOUR HEART.` · `LISTENING TURNS INTO DOING.` · `A RULE IS A WAY OF LISTENING.` · then, large: `HARDEN NOT YOUR HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen with the ear of the heart. Settle, and breathe. Start with the sounds around you. The hum of a room, a car outside, your own breathing. Don't name them, don't judge them. Just lean toward them. Then bring to mind the person you'll talk with next. Plan to give them this same kind of attention: no planning your reply, no checking your phone, just leaning in. If you pray, you can ask to hear God's voice in whatever comes today. The bell holds the time.
Rule. Saint Benedict's short book for monks living together, which opens with one word: listen, with the ear of your heart. Today's word.
Your line: the ear of the heart. Today, listen fully to one person, all the way to the end of what they're saying, before you answer. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns hear passages of the Rule read aloud in community, and oblates and other laypeople read it at home.

original.note: Latin, from the Rule's first sentence: bend down the ear of your heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule is a list of dos and don'ts.
what it means: Benedict's Rule opens with a posture, leaning in to listen with the heart, before any instructions.
what a scholar hears: the Prologue's first sentence, obsculta, o fili, with inclina aurem cordis tui, echoes the language of the Psalms and Proverbs.

notes: The Rule's opening is paraphrased (Gasquet 1909 is the outline's translation, but its exact wording wasn't verified, so nothing is quoted). Latin 'Obsculta (Ausculta), o fili, praecepta magistri, et inclina aurem cordis tui' — confirm spelling and the gloss 'bend down the ear of your heart'.
'Tradition gives the Rule to Saint Benedict, who gathered monks in Italy' — no dates or place names (Subiaco, Monte Cassino) given. Confirm.
The Prologue's use of Psalm 94(95):8 — confirm it is cited there. Douay-Rheims wording to confirm.
'Benedictine monks and nuns still read from the Rule each day' — custom of daily reading (e.g. at chapter); confirm phrasing.
Index word is 'Rule' while the title is 'Listen'; the script uses 'Rule' as today's word as required.

Editor pass: 'read from the Rule each day ... they begin, every time, by being told to listen' was wrong (the Rule is read through in portions, so the Prologue is not heard every day); now 'each time they come back around to its start'; 'each day' dropped from voice and howItsDone; practice 'Imagine' changed to 'Plan to'.
